metadata.file_name: 65. Khine et al. (2024). A Machine-Learning Approach to Predicting the Achievement of Australian Students Using School Climate; Learner Characteristics; and Economic, Social, and Cultural Status.pdf
metadata.title: A Machine-Learning Approach to Predicting the Achievement of Australian Students Using School Climate; Learner Characteristics; and Economic, Social, and Cultural Status

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Australia (15-year-olds) and reports an analytic sample of 13,437 students in 743 schools. The manuscript describes splitting the dataset into 70% training and 30% testing using stratified random sampling, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation. Because the models are standard ML regressors (SVM, KNN, Decision Tree, Elastic Net, XGBoost) implemented via common R/Python packages, the analysis appears to follow an unweighted ML workflow; the paper does not specify any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or complex survey design handling. No additional sample restrictions (e.g., grade bands beyond PISA’s 15-year-old cohort, or exclusions for missingness) are explicitly documented, so the exact missing-data and cleaning rules are unclear beyond the reported final sample size.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is mathematics achievement (ACHIEVE) from PISA 2022, which in PISA is typically represented using plausible values; however, the manuscript does not describe whether plausible values were used directly, averaged, or combined via Rubin’s rules. The paper also does not report any explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap given that questionnaire and background variables commonly have missingness in PISA datasets. As a result, the exact treatment of PVs and missingness cannot be verified from the methods section.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD PISA 2022 data for Australia, focusing on the standard PISA target population of 15-year-old students. The analytic sample comprises 13,437 students in 743 schools who completed the mathematics assessment; the paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the final sample size. For modeling, the dataset was split into 70% training and 30% testing sets using stratified random sampling to preserve proportional representation of classes.

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost: MSE=5227.0, RMSE=72.776, MAE=57.67, MAPE=0.125, R2=0.424 (adjusted R2 highest), correlation coefficient=0.6577; Friedman test: statistic=29.49, p=0.00004922; Nemenyi CD=1.39 indicating XGBoost outperforms others.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for Australian 15-year-olds, the study leveraged self-efficacy (math), socioeconomic status (ESCS), teacher–student interaction, sense of belonging, and disciplinary climate to predict mathematics achievement, finding that XGBoost achieved the lowest prediction errors (MSE/RMSE/MAE/MAPE) and the highest explanatory fit (R2≈0.424) among five regression models. This indicates that strengthening students’ mathematics learning efficacy and addressing socioeconomic disadvantage may improve mathematics outcomes, while SHAP-based feature importance should be interpreted as predictive association rather than causal impact.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Australia (15-year-olds; N=13,437 students in 743 schools) to predict mathematics achievement from school climate and learner characteristics plus ESCS. Five ML regressors were compared using a stratified 70/30 train-test split and hyperparameter tuning: SVM, KNN, Decision Tree, Elastic Net, and XGBoost. Across evaluation metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R2, adjusted R2, and correlation), XGBoost performed best, with MSE=5227.0, RMSE=72.776, MAE=57.67, MAPE=0.125, and R2=0.424 (correlation=0.6577). A Friedman test (p=0.00004922) and Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons supported statistically significant performance differences, with XGBoost notably outperforming the others. The paper uses SHAP (global and local) to interpret feature influence and reports an interaction between MATHEFF and ESCS, but it does not document how plausible values and missing data were handled, and it does not report survey-weighted estimation—so results should be treated as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
